title: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
summary: Why counter++ loses updates across threads, how atomic fetch_add and compare-and-swap make updates indivisible, how CPUs implement them, and what they cost under contention.
outcomes: Explain why a non-atomic counter++ loses updates and why a data race is undefined behavior in C++ and Rust
Use fetch_add and other fetch-and-modify operations and predict the value they return
Write a compare-and-swap retry loop and trace it when another thread interferes
Choose between weak and strong compare-exchange from how LOCK CMPXCHG and LL/SC work
Estimate the cost of contended atomics and prefer a single fetch_add over a CAS loop when possible

lessons.title: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates

blocks.md:
Threads of one process share the same memory (you saw this in the threads course). That is what makes them useful, and also what makes them dangerous: two threads can update the same variable at the same moment.

Take the simplest shared update there is, `counter++`. It looks like one step, but the CPU does three: **read** the value from memory into a register, **add** 1 in the register, and **write** the register back. This is called a *read-modify-write*. If another thread writes between your read and your write, your write overwrites its update.

blocks.caption: Compiler output shown in Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 7. On ARM64 the three steps are visible. The single x86 add is still split into a load and a store inside the core, so it is not atomic across cores either.

blocks.title: Two threads run counter++ once each

scenes.caption: counter starts at 0. Thread A reads it into a register.
Before A writes back, thread B also reads counter. It still sees 0, because A's new value exists only in A's register.
A writes 1. So far so good: memory holds 1.
B writes the 1 it computed from its stale read. Two increments ran, counter is 1: A's update is lost. No error, no crash, just a wrong number.
With an atomic increment, each read-modify-write is one indivisible step. Whatever the order, the second one sees the first one's result and counter ends at 2.

blocks.md: How often does this go wrong? We can count. Model each increment as two steps that touch memory, a read and a write (the add happens in a register). If thread A and thread B each run $n$ such steps, the number of ways to interleave them is a binomial coefficient, because a schedule is just a choice of which of the $2n$ slots belong to A.

blocks.caption: One, two and three increments per thread (n = 2, 4, 6 memory steps). A script ran every schedule and recorded the final counter.

blocks.prompt: Two threads each run counter++ three times, non-atomically, starting from 0. The right answer is 6. What is the smallest final value some schedule can produce?
blocks.reveal: **2**, not 3. One schedule (found by enumerating all 924): A and B both read 0. A writes 1, then reads 1 and writes 2. B now writes its stale 1, erasing A's two increments. A reads 1 for its last increment. B runs its other two increments cleanly up to 3. Finally A writes 2 from its old read, erasing all of B's work. A thread that holds a stale value can overwrite any amount of progress.

blocks.title: Final counter over every schedule (two threads, non-atomic)

scenes.caption: One increment each: 6 schedules. Only the 2 schedules where one thread finishes before the other starts give the right answer, 2.
Two increments each: 70 schedules. Only 6 of them reach 4. Note these are counts of schedules, not probabilities; real timing makes some far likelier than others.
Three increments each: 924 schedules, and only 20 reach the correct 6. Some schedules end at 2, as in the predict above. More increments make a correct result rarer.

blocks.md:
The C++ standard gives this situation a name. Two accesses **conflict** if they touch the same memory location and at least one modifies it. A program has a **data race** if two conflicting actions in different threads are not both atomic and neither *happens before* the other (no synchronization orders them). A data race is **undefined behavior**: not merely a wrong count, but a program the compiler may transform in any way, because it was allowed to assume no other thread touches that variable.

Rust adopts the same rule (its atomics follow the C++20 model), and makes data races impossible without `unsafe` code.

`volatile` does not fix this. In C and C++ it stops the compiler from removing or reordering accesses within one thread, which suits signal handlers and memory-mapped I/O, but cppreference states it is not suitable for communication between threads. A volatile `counter++` is still a separate read and write.
The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

blocks.question: Two threads each run a plain (non-atomic) `counter++` once on a shared counter that starts at 0. Which statement is right?
options: The result is always 2, because each increment is one machine instruction on x86
The result is 1 or 2, and in C or C++ the program has undefined behavior
The result is always 1, because both threads read 0
It is safe as long as the counter is declared volatile
blocks.explain: Depending on the schedule, both reads can happen before either write (result 1) or not (result 2). Being one x86 instruction does not help: the core still loads and stores separately. And since the accesses conflict without synchronization, the C++ standard calls this a data race, which is undefined behavior. volatile does not make it atomic.

lessons.title: Atomic operations: indivisible load, store and fetch_add

blocks.md:
An **atomic** operation is indivisible: every other thread sees it either not started or fully done, never half-way. Conflicting atomic accesses are not a data race, so they are well defined.

C++ provides `std::atomic<T>`; Rust provides types such as `AtomicU32`, `AtomicUsize` and `AtomicBool` in `std::sync::atomic`. All expose the same three families: plain **load** and **store**, **fetch-and-modify** operations, and **compare-and-exchange** (next lesson).

A fetch-and-modify operation changes the variable and returns (fetches) the value it had **before**, all as one atomic step. Rust's list: `fetch_add`, `fetch_sub`, `fetch_and`, `fetch_or`, `fetch_xor`, `fetch_nand`, `fetch_max`, `fetch_min`, plus `swap`, which stores a new value and returns the old one. C++ has `fetch_add`, `fetch_sub`, `fetch_and`, `fetch_or`, `fetch_xor` and `exchange` (C++26 adds `fetch_max` and `fetch_min`), and its `++` and `+=` on an atomic are atomic too.

blocks.caption: From Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 2. Note the method takes &self: atomics are modified through a shared reference.

blocks.md: Every Rust atomic operation takes an `Ordering` argument (C++: `std::memory_order`, default `seq_cst`). This course uses `Relaxed`, which still guarantees that operations on **one** atomic variable are indivisible and consistent, but promises nothing about the order of operations on **different** variables. Ordering gets its own course next.

Because the returned value is the one *before* your add, `fetch_add` hands each caller a distinct number. That makes a unique ID allocator a one-liner. Below, four threads call it in an order chosen by the scheduler.

scenes.caption: NEXT_ID starts at 0. No thread has an ID yet.
T2 happens to run first. Its fetch_add reads 0, writes 1, and returns 0, all in one indivisible step.
T0 runs next and gets 1. It cannot see the 0 again: T2's update is already part of the value it reads.
T3 gets 2 and T1 gets 3. The order depends on scheduling, but the IDs are always 0, 1, 2, 3 with no duplicates and NEXT_ID ends at 4.

blocks.md: Two details matter in practice. First, `fetch_add` and `fetch_sub` **wrap around** on overflow. A `u32` counter wraps after $2^{32} = 4{,}294{,}967{,}296$ calls and hands out 0 again, which a fast machine can reach in seconds. Second, several atomics updated one after another are **not** one atomic update: a reader can see the new item count with the old total time, for example. If several values must change together, use a lock or pack them into one atomic.

blocks.caption: From Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 2.

blocks.question: The allocator above panics once id reaches 1000. Why is it still wrong if callers keep calling it after the panic (say, other threads)?
options: The assert itself is not atomic, so two threads can both pass it with id 999
fetch_add already incremented NEXT_ID before the check, so each later call keeps incrementing it and it eventually wraps back to 0
Relaxed ordering lets a thread read an old NEXT_ID and return a duplicate
Panicking inside a static initializer poisons NEXT_ID
blocks.explain: The check happens after the increment has been committed. Every failing call still bumps NEXT_ID, so after about four billion more calls it wraps to 0 and duplicates appear. Relaxed does not allow duplicates: all fetch_adds on one variable are totally ordered. Fixing this properly needs an operation that can decide not to write, which is what compare-and-swap gives you.

blocks.question: Four threads each add their item count to `done` and their elapsed time to `total_us`, both with fetch_add. A monitor thread loads both and prints total_us / done. What can it observe?
options: Always an exact average, because both variables are atomic
A torn value in done, half old and half new
A crash, because reading two atomics in a row is a data race
A briefly inaccurate average, since the two updates are separate atomic operations
blocks.explain: Each variable is updated atomically, so neither is torn and there is no data race. But nothing makes the pair change together: the monitor can load done after a thread bumped it and total_us before that thread added its time. Mara Bos uses exactly this example; if it matters, put both numbers behind one mutex.

lessons.title: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry

blocks.md:
Fetch-and-modify covers add, or, max and a few more. What about "increment, but not past 1000", or "multiply by 2"? For arbitrary updates you need **compare-and-swap** (CAS), which C++ and Rust call *compare-exchange*.

CAS takes an **expected** value and a **new** value. Atomically, it reads the variable; if it equals expected it writes new and reports success; otherwise it writes nothing and reports failure. Either way it tells you the value it actually found.

blocks.caption: Simplified from Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 2 (memory orderings omitted). The real one is a single atomic operation.

blocks.md: The standard way to use it is the **CAS retry loop**: load the current value, compute the new value from it as if you were alone, then CAS it in. If CAS fails, some other thread changed the variable in between; CAS hands you the value it saw, so you recompute from that and try again. Step through it while thread B interferes:

blocks.title: Thread A increments with a CAS loop while B also increments

scenes.caption: Thread A loads a and sees 5.
A computes new = 6 in a register. Nothing is published yet.
Meanwhile thread B increments a from 5 to 6. A's computation is now based on a stale value.
A's CAS expects 5 but finds 6, so it writes nothing and returns Err(6). This is exactly where plain counter++ would have overwritten B's work.
A loops, recomputing from the value CAS gave it: new = 7.
This time a still holds 6, so the CAS succeeds and a becomes 7. Both increments counted.

blocks.title: The same race as messages to the memory word

scenes.caption: Both threads load a and see 5.
B's CAS(5, 6) wins: a held 5, so it now holds 6.
A's CAS(5, 6) fails because a is no longer 5. The failure carries the current value, so A does not need another load.
A retries with CAS(6, 7) and succeeds. Every failure of a strong CAS means some other thread's write landed, so the system as a whole always makes progress.

blocks.prompt: Earlier, two threads doing 2 non-atomic increments each reached the right answer in only 6 of 70 schedules. Now both use the CAS loop above (load once, then CAS until success). In how many schedules does the counter end at 4?
blocks.reveal: **All of them.** A script that explores every interleaving of the loads and CAS attempts finds 126 distinct executions (more than 70, because failed CAS attempts add retry steps), and every one ends at 4. A thread can only publish a value computed from what is currently in memory.

blocks.md: The loop works for any pure function of the old value, so CAS can implement every other atomic operation. Here is the ID allocator from the last lesson, now checking **before** it writes, so it can never pass the limit:

blocks.caption: From Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 2. Rust also packages this loop as a helper method (fetch_update, renamed try_update in recent releases) that takes a closure.

blocks.md: In C++ the call looks different but does the same thing. `compare_exchange_strong(expected, desired)` returns a `bool`, and on failure it **overwrites your `expected` variable** with the value it found, so the loop body can be empty. The comparison is bitwise, like memcmp, not via `operator==`.

blocks.caption: C++ version of the retry loop. With no ordering argument, both operations default to memory_order_seq_cst.

blocks.md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

Why is CAS the primitive everything else is built on? Herlihy (1991) ranked synchronization primitives by their *consensus number*: how many threads can use the primitive to agree on one value without waiting on each other. Read/write registers reach 1; test-and-set, swap and fetch-and-add reach 2; compare-and-swap is unbounded. So with CAS you can build a wait-free version of any shared object for any number of threads, which fetch_add alone cannot do.

blocks.question: From cppreference: `std::atomic<int> ai = 3; int tst_val = 4, new_val = 5;` then `bool ok = ai.compare_exchange_strong(tst_val, new_val);`. What are ai, tst_val and ok afterwards?
options: ai = 5, tst_val = 4, ok = true
ai = 3, tst_val = 4, ok = false
ai = 3, tst_val = 3, ok = false
ai = 4, tst_val = 3, ok = false
blocks.explain: ai (3) differs from tst_val (4), so nothing is stored and the call returns false. On failure the C++ API copies the value it found into the expected argument, so tst_val becomes 3. Calling it again now succeeds: ai becomes 5 and ok is true.

blocks.question: A teammate writes a CAS loop to double a shared value but calls `a.load()` again inside the loop and ignores the Err value. Is it correct?
options: Yes, it is correct; using the Err value only saves a redundant load
No: reloading reintroduces the lost-update race
No: a CAS loop must use the Err value or it can livelock forever
Yes, but only with SeqCst ordering
blocks.explain: Correctness comes from the CAS: it only writes if the variable still equals the expected value you computed from. Where that expected value came from (a fresh load or the Err payload) does not matter. Using the returned value just avoids an extra memory access.

lessons.title: Inside the CPU: LOCK CMPXCHG, LL/SC, and weak versus strong

blocks.md: **x86.** Intel added a `lock` instruction prefix that makes certain read-modify-write instructions atomic. Intel's manual lists the instructions it may prefix, all with a memory destination: ADD, ADC, AND, BTC, BTR, BTS, CMPXCHG, CMPXCHG8B, CMPXCHG16B, DEC, INC, NEG, NOT, OR, SBB, SUB, XOR, XADD and XCHG. XCHG is always locked, prefix or not. Early processors asserted a bus-wide LOCK# signal; since the P6 family, if the data is cached the processor only locks that cache line and relies on cache coherence to keep the operation atomic.

`cmpxchg` is CAS in one instruction: it compares the accumulator register (EAX or RAX) with memory; if equal it stores the source register and sets the zero flag, otherwise it loads memory into the accumulator. `xadd` is fetch-and-add. When an operation has no matching instruction, such as `fetch_or` whose old value you use, the compiler emits a CAS loop:

blocks.code:
; x.fetch_add(10, Relaxed), result used
    mov  eax, 10
    lock xadd dword ptr [rdi], eax   ; eax = old value

; x.fetch_or(10, Relaxed), result used
    mov  eax, dword ptr [rdi]
.L1:
    mov  ecx, eax
    or   ecx, 10
    lock cmpxchg dword ptr [rdi], ecx ; expected in eax, new in ecx
    jne  .L1                          ; ZF clear: failed, eax = current
blocks.caption: x86-64 output for Rust code, from Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 7. A hand-written compare_exchange loop doing the same OR compiles to identical code on x86-64.

blocks.md: **ARM64 and other RISC designs** use a pair of instructions instead: **load-linked / store-conditional** (LL/SC). On ARM64 they are `ldxr` (load exclusive) and `stxr` (store exclusive). The load starts watching the address; the store only happens if nothing has written there since, and it reports success (0) or failure (1) in a register. Two rules keep the hardware simple: a core watches one address at a time, and the store may **fail even if nobody wrote the value** (a false negative), for instance because the hardware tracks a whole block of memory rather than one variable, or the reservation was lost. ARMv8.1 later added single instructions such as `cas` and `ldadd`.

blocks.title: A strong compare_exchange(5, 6) on ARM64 (LL/SC)
blocks.code:
mov  w8, #6           // new value
.L1:
    ldxr w9, [x0]         // load-exclusive: read, start watching
    cmp  w9, #5           // equal to expected?
    b.ne .L2
    stxr w9, w8, [x0]     // store-exclusive: w9 = 0 ok, 1 refused
    cbnz w9, .L1          // refused? start over (strong CAS only)
    ret
.L2:
    clrex                 // values differ: stop watching
    ret

scenes.caption: The new value 6 goes into w8 once, outside the loop, to keep the watched window short.
ldxr reads 5 and starts watching the address (the exclusive monitor is armed).
5 equals the expected value, so no branch to .L2.
Suppose the reservation is lost before the store, which LL/SC allows even when nobody wrote the value. stxr refuses to write and sets w9 = 1, even though the value is still 5: a spurious failure.
Strong CAS must not report a failure the value did not cause, so cbnz jumps back and the whole attempt restarts.
Second try: ldxr reads 5 again, the comparison passes, and stxr succeeds (w9 = 0). Memory now holds 6.
Success, return. compare_exchange_weak compiles to the same code without the retry branch: it would have returned the spurious failure to you instead of retrying.

blocks.md:
That is why two CAS flavors exist. `compare_exchange_weak` **may fail spuriously**: it can report failure even when the value matched. That lets it map straight onto one LL/SC attempt. `compare_exchange` (C++: `compare_exchange_strong`) only fails if the value really differed, so on LL/SC machines it hides an inner retry loop.

On x86-64, and on ARM64 when the `cas` instruction is used, both compile to the same single instruction. GCC's builtin documentation adds that many targets only offer the strong variation and ignore the weak flag.

blocks.title: What common atomic operations compile to

nodes.label:
ldxr, add, stxr loop
or ldadd (v8.1)

scenes.caption: fetch_add has a dedicated instruction on x86-64 (xadd) and on ARMv8.1 (ldadd). On ARMv8.0 it is a short LL/SC loop.
compare_exchange is one instruction on x86-64 (cmpxchg) and ARMv8.1 (cas); there weak and strong are identical. With LL/SC, strong adds a retry branch.

x86-64 has no instruction for a multi-bit fetch_or that returns the old value (single-bit cases can use lock bts), so the compiler writes a CAS loop for you. Atomics are lock-free, but not every operation is a single step.

blocks.md: Rule of thumb from the docs: use `compare_exchange_weak` inside a loop that retries anyway (a spurious failure just costs one more iteration), and `compare_exchange` (strong) for a single attempt whose failure you act on. When in doubt, GCC's manual says to use strong.

blocks.question: get_key() lazily creates a random key: if KEY is 0, generate one and CAS it from 0 to the new key; if the CAS fails, use the key another thread stored. There is no loop. Which CAS should it use?
options: compare_exchange_weak, because it is faster on ARM
Either, since x86 and ARM compile them identically
compare_exchange (strong), because a spurious failure would make it return 0 as the key
Neither; it needs fetch_add
blocks.explain: With weak, the CAS could fail even though KEY was still 0, and the Err would carry 0, which the function would return as the key. Strong only fails if another thread really installed a key. Weak is for loops where a spurious failure just means one more iteration. And on LL/SC targets (ARMv8.0) the two do compile differently.

blocks.question: Rust's docs say atomic types are lock-free but not guaranteed wait-free. What does that mean for `x.fetch_or(mask, Relaxed)` with the result used, on x86-64?
options: It may take a hidden global mutex if the CPU lacks an instruction
It is always exactly one instruction, so it is wait-free
It may return a torn, half-updated value
It may run as a CAS loop, so under contention one call can take several attempts
blocks.explain: Lock-free means no hidden global mutex. But x86-64 has no single instruction for fetch_or that returns the old value, so it compiles to a lock cmpxchg loop, and a thread can lose several rounds to others. The result is never torn: each attempt is atomic.

lessons.title: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses

blocks.md: Atomics are not free, and the cost comes mostly from caches, not from the instruction. Each core has private caches holding 64-byte *cache lines*, kept consistent by a coherence protocol such as MESI. Many cores may hold a clean copy of a line for reading, but to **modify** it a core needs **exclusive** ownership, which invalidates every other copy. An atomic read-modify-write must own the line for its duration, so when several cores hammer one atomic, the line bounces from core to core.

Mara Bos measured this in *Rust Atomics and Locks*: one thread does a billion relaxed loads of an `AtomicU64` while a background thread touches the same variable. A background thread that only **loads** made no significant difference (about 300 ms either way on an older x86-64 machine). A background thread that **stores** made the loads about ten times slower, because every store steals the line.

blocks.title: A billion loads, alone and with another core storing to the line

scenes.caption: Older x86-64 machine: about 300 ms alone, about 3 s while another core stores to the same variable. Approximate figures as reported by Mara Bos; yours will differ.
Newer chips suffer less but still visibly: an Apple M1 went from 350 to 500 ms, and a recent AMD processor from 250 to 650 ms.

blocks.prompt: Replace the background thread's store with a compare_exchange(10, 20) that never succeeds, because the variable is always 0. It never writes anything. Do the main thread's loads stay fast?
blocks.reveal: **No.** On most architectures a CAS claims exclusive access to the cache line whether or not the comparison succeeds, so a failing CAS slows other cores much like a store. Intel's manual even says that with LOCK CMPXCHG the destination receives a write cycle regardless of the comparison result (it writes back the old value on failure). This is why spin loops should **load** the value first and only attempt the CAS when it looks like it can succeed.

blocks.md: Contention also multiplies attempts. Consider a simplified model: $N$ threads each want to add 1 using a CAS loop, and they move in lockstep. In each round, all remaining threads load the same value and try to CAS; exactly one wins and the rest fail and retry. With fetch_add, each thread needs exactly one operation.

blocks.caption: For N = 4: 10 attempts versus 4. For N = 8: 36 versus 8, of which 28 are failures that still grabbed the cache line.

blocks.title: Lockstep model: CAS attempts versus fetch_add operations

scenes.caption: With fetch_add every operation succeeds, so work grows linearly with the number of threads.

A CAS loop wastes the failed attempts, and they grow quadratically in this worst-case lockstep model: 136 attempts for 16 threads. Simplified: real threads are not in lockstep, so the waste is usually smaller, but the trend under heavy contention is real.

blocks.md: Use the most specific operation that does the job. If a fetch_add, fetch_or or swap expresses your update, prefer it to a hand-written CAS loop: it never fails, and on ARM the compiler turns it into a tight instruction sequence, which (as of Mara Bos's tests) it does not do for a hand-written CAS loop.

Where you meet these operations in real code:

- **Reference counts.** Rust's `Arc::clone` increments its count with an atomic add and aborts the process if the count would overflow.
- **Counters, IDs and statistics**, as in lesson 2.
- **Lazy one-time initialization**: CAS a pointer or key from "empty" to a value; the loser uses the winner's value. In real code prefer `std::sync::OnceLock` or `std::call_once`.
- **Locks.** A mutex or spinlock is acquired by atomically changing a flag from unlocked to locked, typically with CAS or swap; this is the next course on mutexes.
- **Lock-free data structures**, such as a stack whose `push` CASes the head pointer from the old node to the new one.

blocks.question: Eight threads spin waiting for a lock flag to become 0, each running `while lock.compare_exchange(0, 1, ...).is_err() {}`. The lock is held for a long time. What is the main performance problem?
options: Each failing CAS still takes exclusive ownership of the flag's cache line, so the waiters keep stealing it from each other and from the holder
compare_exchange cannot fail, so the loop never ends
The CAS writes 1 even when it fails, so it corrupts the lock
Nothing; failed CAS attempts are as cheap as loads
blocks.explain: A failed CAS does not change the value, but it still demands exclusive access to the line, so eight spinners bounce it between cores and slow down the holder too. The usual fix is to spin on a plain load until the flag reads 0 and only then try the CAS (test and test-and-set).

blocks.question: You need a shared counter of processed requests, incremented by 32 worker threads. Which choice fits best?
options: A CAS loop, because CAS is the most general primitive
A mutex around a plain integer, because atomics are undefined behavior with more than two threads
fetch_add(1, Relaxed), because it never retries and expresses exactly the update
A volatile integer with ++
blocks.explain: fetch_add does the whole read-modify-write in one operation that cannot fail, so there are no wasted attempts under contention. A CAS loop is correct but retries under contention. A mutex works but costs more. volatile ++ is a data race.
